title: My Husband Spent $73,000 on a Secret House. Then the Agent Asked Why I Was Listed as the Seller (PART 2) – Story Loom
excerpt: I didn’t speak for a long time. The man in the photograph was named Walter Greene. The baby in his arms was me.
author: admin

blocks.text: I didn’t speak for a long time. The man in the photograph was named Walter Greene. The baby in his arms was me.
I drove to my mother’s house that night. She’s seventy-six. When I put the photo on her table, she started crying before I said a word.

In 1977, before she married the man I’d always called Dad, my mother fell in love with Walter, a fisherman in Florida, the summer she worked there as a waitress. She got pregnant. Walter wanted to marry her. Her parents refused and brought her home to Ohio. She married my dad, a kind man who knew everything and raised me as his own. Walter never married. He sent birthday cards to my mother every year, asking about me. She kept them in a hatbox.
When Walter died in 2016, he left his small beach house to me. The estate lawyer sent letters to my mother’s old address and then to mine. My husband, Greg, collects our mail.

My attorney pieced together the rest. Greg opened the letters, realized what they meant, and decided not to tell me. He waited until he had debts he couldn’t explain, then hired a notary who didn’t look closely and forged my signature on the sale documents. The house sold for $640,000. The money went into an account in his name. The $73,000 from our joint savings was the down payment on a condo in another part of Florida. He was planning to leave me and start fresh on my inheritance.

Because my signature was forged, the sale was invalid. The buyers had title insurance, and they were made whole. The house came back to me. Greg’s account was frozen. The notary lost her commission. Greg is facing charges for forgery and fraud, and the divorce went quickly once his lawyer saw the evidence.

In March, my mother and I drove down to Florida together. The house is small and blue, with a porch facing the water. Inside, on the mantel, was a framed photograph of a baby in a sun hat. Me. Walter had kept it there for forty-eight years.
My mother walked down to the beach and stood there a long time. When she came back, she said, “He used to say he’d wait for me on this porch.” I said, “I think he did.”
I’m keeping the house. My mother spends the winters there now. And on the porch, I put a new nameplate by the door: GREENE.
